tool.name: MahalanobisChiSquare
tool.summary: Transforms a Mahalanobis squared-distance (D2) raster into a chi-square typicality p-value raster, rescaling the unbounded D2 values to a 0 to 1 probability where values near 1 indicate a close match to the reference conditions.
tool.usage:
For every cell, the output is the upper-tail chi-square probability p = P(chi-square > D2), evaluated with degrees of freedom equal to the number of variables that produced the D2 raster. Mahalanobis distances have no upper bound; this transform recodes them onto a fixed 0 to 1 scale, and because the transform is monotonic it also inverts the order: high D2 (dissimilar) becomes a low p-value, and low D2 (similar) becomes a high p-value.
The transform is computed cell-by-cell (block vectorized) so it stays memory-bounded for large rasters; NoData cells remain NoData.
The input must be a squared-distance (D2) raster, not a Distance (D) or already-transformed p-value raster. When the D2 raster was created by the Mahalanobis Distance Raster tool, its number of variables (the degrees of freedom) is recorded in the raster metadata and pre-filled here automatically; a warning is shown if the input metadata indicates it is not a D2 raster.
Note on degrees of freedom. This tool uses the statistically standard value, df = number of variables (Mardia, Kent and Bibby 1979; Seber 1984). Some ecological sources instead use number of variables minus 1 (Clark et al. 1993; Farber and Kadmon 2003). Because the transform is monotonic in D2, the choice only rescales the p-values and never changes the ranking of cells; set the degrees of freedom accordingly if you wish to reproduce those sources.
Reference: Mahalanobis, P.C. (1936). On the generalised distance in statistics. Proceedings of the National Institute of Sciences of India 2(1):49-55.
Additional reading: Clark et al. (1993), Knick and Dyer (1997), and Farber and Kadmon (2002) illustrate the chi-square rescaling of Mahalanobis distances in ecological applications and discuss its normality assumption.

dialogReference.para: The Mahalanobis squared-distance (D2) raster to rescale. Use a raster of D2 values, not Distance (D) or an already-transformed p-value raster.

If this raster was produced by the Mahalanobis Distance Raster tool, its variable count is read from the metadata and used to pre-fill the degrees of freedom below; a warning appears if the metadata shows the raster is not a D2 surface.

The chi-square degrees of freedom, which equal the number of variables used to build the D2 raster. This is pre-filled automatically when the input raster's metadata records it; otherwise enter the number of variables.

This tool uses the statistically standard value, df = number of variables. Some ecological sources (Clark et al. 1993; Farber and Kadmon 2003) use number of variables minus 1; because the transform is monotonic in D2, this only rescales the p-values and never changes the ranking of cells. Set the value yourself if you wish to match those sources.

The output chi-square p-value raster (0 to 1, values near 1 indicating a close match to the reference conditions). Defaults to Mahalanobis_Pvalue in the current workspace, auto-incremented if that name is already taken.

scriptExample.title: MahalanobisChiSquare example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Rescale a three-variable Mahalanobis D2 raster to a chi-square typicality p-value (df = 3).
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.MahalanobisChiSquare( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Mahalanobis.gdb\Mahalanobis", df=3, out_raster=r"C:\Project\Mahalanobis.gdb\Mahalanobis_Pvalue")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Rescales a Mahalanobis squared-distance (D2) raster to a 0 to 1 chi-square typicality p-value.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Transforms a Mahalanobis squared-distance (D2) raster into a chi-square typicality p-value raster. For each cell the output is the upper-tail probability P(chi-square greater than D2), with degrees of freedom equal to the number of variables; the result is a 0 to 1 surface where values near 1 indicate a close match to the reference conditions. Degrees of freedom are pre-filled from the input raster's metadata when it was created by the Mahalanobis Raster tool. This tool uses the statistically standard df = number of variables; some ecological sources (Clark et al. 1993; Farber and Kadmon 2003) use number of variables minus 1.
